title: The heart: chambers, valves and coronaries
summary: Follow one red cell round, then work out which artery is blocked.

steps.title: The four chambers
steps.text:
Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium from the venae cavae and coronary sinus, crosses the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and is pumped through the pulmonary valve to the lungs.

It returns to the left atrium by four pulmonary veins, crosses the mitral valve into the left ventricle – whose wall is three times thicker – and leaves through the aortic valve.

check.q: Which chamber lies most anteriorly, and which forms the apex?
check.a: The right ventricle is most anterior; the left ventricle forms the apex.

steps.title: The valves and where you listen
steps.text:
The four valves sit in the fibrous skeleton in an oblique plane, but you listen downstream of each:
Aortic – right 2nd intercostal space.
Pulmonary – left 2nd space.
Tricuspid – left lower sternal edge.
Mitral – 5th space in the midclavicular line, the apex.

All Physicians Take Money.

check.q: Where do you listen for the mitral valve, and why is it not over the valve itself?
check.a: At the apex, in the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line — sound is carried downstream in the direction of blood flow.

steps.title: The coronary arteries
steps.text:
Both arise from the aortic sinuses just above the valve. Left ventricular coronary flow is greatest in diastole, when myocardial compression of the vessels relaxes; tachycardia shortens that opportunity.

The left coronary divides into the anterior interventricular (LAD) and circumflex. The right runs in the right atrioventricular groove, giving the SA nodal branch in 60% of people, the AV nodal branch in about 90% (right dominance), and the posterior interventricular artery.

check.q: Which artery supplies the anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum?
check.a: The anterior interventricular (left anterior descending) branch of the left coronary artery.

steps.title: Reading the infarct
steps.text:
LAD – anterior wall and anterior two-thirds of the septum: ST elevation in V1–V4. The 'widow-maker'.
Circumflex – lateral wall: I, aVL, V5–V6.
Right coronary – inferior wall: II, III, aVF; often with bradycardia and heart block because it usually supplies both nodes, and with right ventricular infarction, in which nitrates are dangerous.

check.q: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which artery?
check.a: The right coronary artery — an inferior infarct.

steps.title: Cardiac muscle up close
steps.text: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle but branched, with one or two central nuclei and intercalated discs that carry both the desmosomes holding cells together and the gap junctions that let them fire as one.

steps.title: The pressure opens the valve
steps.text:
A valve opens when pressure behind it exceeds pressure ahead of it, and closes when the gradient reverses. During ventricular filling, atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure and the atrioventricular valves open. As ventricular contraction begins, the rising pressure closes them.

Papillary muscles contract with the ventricles and tension the chordae tendineae, preventing the AV leaflets from being pushed back into the atria. They do not pull the valves open. Aortic and pulmonary valves have no chordae; their cusp shape and the pressure gradient allow closure.

check.q: Do papillary muscles open the mitral valve by pulling on its chordae?
check.a: No. Pressure differences open the valve; papillary muscles stabilise the leaflets against prolapse during ventricular contraction.

objectives: Follow blood through the four chambers and four valves
Locate the valves and their auscultation areas
Relate the coronary arteries to the chambers they supply
Explain passive valve opening and the role of papillary muscles during systole
takeaways: Right atrium → tricuspid → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → lungs → left atrium → mitral → left ventricle → aortic valve.
Valves are heard downstream of where they lie, along the direction of blood flow.
The left ventricle forms the apex; the right ventricle is the most anterior chamber.
Pressure differences open and close valves; papillary muscles tension chordae to prevent AV valve prolapse, rather than pulling the valves open.

title: The bronchial tree and lung lobes
summary: Why an inhaled peanut goes to the right, and where it lands.

steps.title: Trachea to bronchi
steps.text: The trachea bifurcates at the carina, level with the sternal angle (T4/5). The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled foreign bodies and aspirated material go right – classically to the posterior segment of the upper lobe when supine, or the superior segment of the lower lobe.

check.q: At what level does the trachea divide, and why does an inhaled object go right?
check.a: At the carina, level with the sternal angle; the right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical.

steps.title: Lobes and fissures
steps.text:
The right lung has three lobes: oblique and horizontal fissures. The left has two, an oblique fissure only, plus the lingula and a cardiac notch where the heart sits.

Surface marking: the oblique fissure follows the line of the 6th rib; the horizontal fissure runs along the 4th costal cartilage. Listen over the upper front for upper lobe, the axilla for middle/lingula, and the back for lower lobe.

check.q: Which lung has three lobes, and what is the left lung's equivalent of the middle lobe?
check.a: The right; the lingula, part of the left upper lobe.

steps.title: Bronchopulmonary segments
steps.text: Each lung has about ten bronchopulmonary segments, each with its own segmental bronchus and artery, and veins in the planes between them. Because of that they can be resected individually – the basis of segmentectomy and of postural drainage.

check.q: What makes a bronchopulmonary segment surgically resectable?
check.a: It has its own segmental bronchus and artery, with its veins running between segments.

steps.title: The gas-exchange surface
steps.text: The conducting airways end at the terminal bronchiole; beyond it lies the acinus, where gas exchange happens across a barrier less than a micrometre thick. Open the microanatomy model and look at the capillaries running over the alveolar walls.

steps.title: The wall changes before the air reaches an alveolus
steps.text:
In the trachea, C-shaped cartilage supports the airway. In intrapulmonary bronchi, cartilage becomes irregular plates and the wall still contains glands. Bronchioles lack both cartilage and submucosal glands; their smooth muscle can substantially change airway calibre.

A terminal bronchiole is the last purely conducting airway. A respiratory bronchiole has alveoli opening from its wall, so exchange begins before the alveolar ducts and sacs are reached. Bronchiole is a structural category, not just an informal word for any small bronchus.

check.q: Which two supporting features present in bronchi are absent from bronchioles?
check.a: Cartilage and submucosal glands.

steps.title: Two alveolar cells divide the work
steps.text:
Type I pneumocytes are very thin cells covering most of the alveolar surface. Along with the capillary endothelium and thin intervening basement membranes, they form the short diffusion path for gases.

Type II pneumocytes are more cuboidal and secrete surfactant, which reduces surface tension at the air-liquid interface and helps keep alveoli open. They also contribute to epithelial repair. The most extensive surface cell and the main surfactant-producing cell are therefore different cell types.

check.q: Which alveolar cell mainly provides the thin gas-exchange surface, and which produces surfactant?
check.a: Type I provides most of the thin surface; type II produces surfactant.

objectives: Trace the airway from trachea to bronchiole
Explain why inhaled objects go to the right
Match lobar bronchi to the lobes they supply
Distinguish bronchi from bronchioles and type I from type II alveolar cells
takeaways: The trachea divides at the carina, at the level of the sternal angle.
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical.
Ten bronchopulmonary segments on the right; eight to ten on the left.
Bronchi contain cartilage and glands; bronchioles lack them. Type I alveolar cells form thin exchange surfaces and type II cells produce surfactant.

title: The coeliac trunk and the foregut
summary: Three branches, and why foregut pain is felt in the epigastrium.

steps.title: Three arteries, three guts
steps.text:
Coeliac trunk (T12) supplies the foregut – to the second part of the duodenum, plus liver, spleen and pancreas.
Superior mesenteric (L1) supplies the midgut – to two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon.
Inferior mesenteric (L3) supplies the hindgut – to the upper rectum.

Each is a midline branch of the abdominal aorta, and each is matched by a band of referred pain: epigastric, periumbilical, suprapubic.

check.q: Which three arteries supply the gut, and which part does each supply?
check.a: Coeliac trunk — foregut; superior mesenteric — midgut; inferior mesenteric — hindgut.

steps.title: The coeliac trunk's three branches
steps.text: Left gastric, splenic and common hepatic. The left gastric anastomoses with the right along the lesser curve; the splenic runs along the top of the pancreas giving short gastrics and the left gastro-omental; the common hepatic gives the gastroduodenal artery – which lies behind the first part of the duodenum and bleeds catastrophically from a posterior ulcer.

check.q: Name the three branches of the coeliac trunk.
check.a: Left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries.

steps.title: The stomach
steps.text:
Cardia, fundus, body, pyloric antrum and pylorus. Its blood supply comes from both curvatures; its venous drainage goes to the portal system, and lymph from the lower third can reach the left supraclavicular node – Virchow's node, Troisier's sign.

Look at the gastric mucosa: the pits, the parietal cells that make acid and the chief cells that make pepsinogen.

steps.title: Referred pain
steps.text:
Foregut, midgut and hindgut have no somatic innervation, so their pain is dull, midline and poorly localised at the level of their sympathetic supply.

Appendicitis is the classic demonstration: it starts periumbilical (midgut visceral pain) and moves to the right iliac fossa only when the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal peritoneum, which is somatically innervated and precisely localised.

check.q: Where is foregut pain felt, and why?
check.a: In the epigastrium — visceral afferents run back with the sympathetic supply to T6–T9.

steps.title: Two gut territories meet around the pancreatic head
steps.text:
The gastroduodenal artery gives superior pancreaticoduodenal branches to the pancreatic head and adjoining duodenum. Inferior pancreaticoduodenal branches rise from the superior mesenteric circulation. They meet in arcades around the same region.

This is an anatomical link across the foregut-midgut boundary, which lies near the entry of the bile duct into the descending duodenum. Embryological territories explain the overall supply, but communicating arcades make the adult boundary less like a sharp line drawn through a tube.

check.q: Which arterial arcade links the coeliac and superior mesenteric territories around the duodenum?
check.a: The pancreaticoduodenal arcades, joining superior branches from the gastroduodenal artery with inferior branches from the SMA.

steps.title: An arterial territory is not an embryological identity
steps.text:
The spleen receives the splenic artery from the coeliac trunk, but it does not develop from the gut endoderm like the lining of the foregut. It develops from mesenchyme within the dorsal mesogastrium and becomes closely related to the stomach.

Its shared arterial neighbourhood therefore does not make it a digestive gland. The liver and pancreas have digestive secretory functions; the spleen filters blood and participates in immune responses. Keep blood supply, developmental origin and adult function as three related but separate ways of classifying an organ.

check.q: Does coeliac arterial supply make the spleen an endoderm-derived digestive organ?
check.a: No. It develops from mesenchyme in the dorsal mesogastrium and is a lymphoid, blood-filtering organ.

objectives: Name the three branches of the coeliac trunk and their distribution
Define the extent of the foregut
Explain why foregut pain is felt in the epigastrium
Explain the pancreaticoduodenal connection between coeliac and superior mesenteric circulations
takeaways: Left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries, at T12.
Foregut runs from the oesophagus to the middle of the second part of the duodenum.
Foregut pain is referred to the epigastrium, midgut to the umbilicus, hindgut to the suprapubic area.
Superior pancreaticoduodenal branches from the gastroduodenal artery connect with inferior branches from the SMA around the pancreatic head and duodenum.

title: The portal venous system
summary: Where the blood goes when the liver will not take it.

steps.title: Formation
steps.text: The portal vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. It carries about 75% of the liver's blood flow – nutrient-rich and less oxygenated than arterial blood, but still an important source of hepatic oxygen – and runs in the free edge of the lesser omentum, behind the bile duct and hepatic artery.

check.q: Which two veins unite to form the portal vein, and where?
check.a: The splenic and superior mesenteric veins, behind the neck of the pancreas.

steps.title: Portosystemic anastomoses
steps.text:
When portal pressure rises the blood finds the four places where portal and systemic veins meet:
Lower oesophagus – left gastric to azygos: oesophageal varices, which bleed.
Rectum – superior to middle/inferior rectal: anorectal varices, distinct from ordinary haemorrhoidal disease.
Umbilicus – paraumbilical to epigastric veins: caput medusae.
Retroperitoneum – veins of Retzius.

check.q: Name three sites of portosystemic anastomosis.
check.a: Lower oesophagus, the umbilicus (caput medusae), the rectum, and the retroperitoneum — any three.

steps.title: Inside the liver
steps.text:
Blood from the portal triads runs through sinusoids to the central vein of each lobule, so the periportal hepatocytes (zone 1) get the best oxygen and the centrilobular ones (zone 3) the worst.

Zone 3 is especially vulnerable to reduced perfusion. It is also vulnerable in paracetamol toxicity because of local drug metabolism. Viral hepatitis does not follow a universal zone-1-first pattern.

check.q: Which acinar zone is most vulnerable to reduced perfusion, and why?
check.a: Zone 3, near the central vein, receives blood after it has passed through upstream sinusoids and therefore has the lowest oxygen supply.

steps.title: Two capillary beds before the heart
steps.text:
An ordinary systemic route runs artery, capillary bed, vein, heart. The hepatic portal system inserts a second capillary bed: blood leaving digestive-organ capillaries travels through portal tributaries and the portal vein into the liver sinusoids before returning to the heart.

That arrangement delivers absorbed substances to hepatocytes early, supporting storage, metabolic processing and modification of many ingested compounds. The blood has already exchanged gases in one tissue, but still supplies a substantial amount of the liver's oxygen because its volume of flow is large.

check.q: What makes the hepatic portal vein part of a portal system?
check.a: It connects one capillary bed in abdominal organs to a second in the liver before blood returns to the heart.

steps.title: The vein entering is not the veins leaving
steps.text:
The portal vein enters the liver at the porta hepatis and divides alongside the hepatic arterial and biliary branches. The hepatic veins collect sinusoidal outflow and drain into the inferior vena cava on the posterior side of the liver.

Portal inflow obstruction and hepatic venous outflow obstruction therefore occur on opposite sides of the sinusoidal network, even though both can raise pressure within the portal circulation. On the model, separate the incoming portal trunk from the veins leaving the organ rather than calling all liver veins portal veins.

check.q: Which vessels carry blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava?
check.a: The hepatic veins, not the portal vein.

objectives: Name the tributaries that form the portal vein
List the sites of portosystemic anastomosis
Explain the clinical signs of portal hypertension
Distinguish portal venous inflow from hepatic venous outflow and explain the portal system as two capillary beds in series
takeaways: Splenic vein plus superior mesenteric vein, behind the neck of the pancreas.
Portosystemic sites: lower oesophagus, umbilicus, rectum and the retroperitoneum.
Oesophageal varices, caput medusae and anorectal varices reflect portal collateral flow; ordinary haemorrhoidal disease is distinct.
Portal blood passes through digestive-organ capillaries and then liver sinusoids; hepatic veins drain the liver into the IVC.

title: The kidney and the retroperitoneum
summary: Relations, the three constrictions of the ureter, and how urine is made.

steps.title: Position and coverings
steps.text:
Retroperitoneal, from about T12 to L3, the right lower than the left because of the liver. From inside out: capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, pararenal fat.

At the hilum, front to back: Vein, Artery, Ureter.

check.q: At what vertebral levels do the kidneys lie, and why is the right lower?
check.a: T12 to L3; the right is pushed down by the liver.

steps.title: The ureter
steps.text:
It runs down on psoas major, crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and turns forward to enter the bladder obliquely – the oblique course is the valve that prevents reflux.

Three constrictions, where stones lodge: the pelvi-ureteric junction, the pelvic brim, and the vesico-ureteric junction. Pain is referred from loin to groin.

check.q: Name the three constrictions of the ureter.
check.a: The pelvi-ureteric junction, the crossing of the pelvic brim, and the vesico-ureteric junction.

steps.title: The nephron
steps.text:
A million per kidney. Filtration in the glomerulus, bulk reabsorption in the proximal tubule, the countercurrent multiplier in the loop of Henle, fine adjustment in the distal tubule and collecting duct under aldosterone and ADH.

Open the model, then use its Nephron and Corpuscle views to follow one nephron from its renal corpuscle to the collecting duct.

check.q: Which part of the nephron reabsorbs most of the filtered load?
check.a: The proximal convoluted tubule — around two thirds of the filtered sodium and water.

steps.title: The bladder and the urothelium
steps.text: The trigone is smooth and mesodermal; the rest of the bladder is wrinkled into rugae and lined by urothelium, whose umbrella cells and tight junctions hold urine at bay while the wall stretches.

check.q: What kind of epithelium lines the bladder, and why?
check.a: Urothelium (transitional epithelium) — it stretches and is impermeable to urine.

steps.title: A pyramid drains through its tip
steps.text:
The renal cortex lies outside the medullary pyramids. Collecting ducts run towards the apex of a pyramid, the renal papilla, and empty through papillary ducts into a minor calyx. Several minor calyces join into larger calyces.

These feed the funnel-shaped renal pelvis, which narrows into the ureter. The calyces and pelvis collect urine; they are not vessels carrying renal blood. Follow the kidney towards its hilum and keep the venous, arterial and collecting-system routes separate.

check.q: What receives urine directly from the papillary ducts at the tip of a renal pyramid?
check.a: A minor calyx.

steps.title: Blood leaves a glomerulus through another arteriole
steps.text:
Blood enters a glomerular capillary tuft through an afferent arteriole and leaves through an efferent arteriole. The efferent vessel then supplies peritubular capillaries, or the vasa recta associated with long-looped nephrons, before blood returns through the venous system.

Filtrate takes a different route: across the filtration barrier into Bowman's space, then along the nephron tubule. Reabsorbed water and solutes move from that tubular route back towards the surrounding blood vessels. Draw two paths in the microanatomy model, one for blood and one for tubular fluid.

check.q: Does blood leaving the glomerulus normally flow into the proximal tubule?
check.a: No. Blood leaves through the efferent arteriole; filtered fluid enters the tubular pathway.

objectives: Describe the position, coverings and relations of the kidney
Trace the ureter and its constrictions
Outline how the nephron makes urine
Trace urine from the collecting ducts to the renal pelvis and distinguish filtrate flow from renal blood flow
takeaways: The kidneys lie at T12–L3, the right slightly lower because of the liver.
Coverings from inside out: capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, pararenal fat.
The renal hilum contains vein, artery and pelvis from front to back.
Urine passes from papillary ducts through minor and major calyces to the renal pelvis; renal blood exits through veins, not the collecting system.

title: Skin, from the outside in
summary: The layers that burns, blisters and biopsies are described by.

steps.title: What the dissection slider removes first
steps.text: Skin is the body's largest organ and the first thing a dissection takes off. Slide the dissection control on the View tab from 0 upwards and watch the surface go before anything else.

steps.title: Epidermis and dermis
steps.text:
Epidermis: stratified squamous keratinised epithelium – basale, spinosum, granulosum, (lucidum in thick skin), corneum. Turnover takes about a month.
Dermis: papillary and reticular layers carrying the vessels, nerves, follicles and glands.

Blisters tell you the level: pemphigus splits within the epidermis and is flaccid; pemphigoid lifts the whole epidermis off the basement membrane and is tense.

check.q: Name the layers of the epidermis from the base upwards.
check.a: Stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, (lucidum in thick skin) and corneum.

steps.title: Thick skin, and why fingerprints exist
steps.text: Palms and soles have a stratum lucidum, a far thicker corneum, no hair follicles, and epidermal ridges over dermal papillae packed with Meissner corpuscles – the ridges are what leaves a fingerprint.

check.q: Why can a superficial partial-thickness burn heal without grafting?
check.a: Epithelial stem cells survive in the hair follicles and sweat glands deep in the dermis.

steps.title: The outer layer has no vessels
steps.text:
The epidermis is avascular. Its living cells receive oxygen and nutrients by diffusion from capillaries in the underlying dermis, especially the loops approaching the dermal papillae. Vessels do not run up through every epidermal layer to the surface.

Basal keratinocytes divide and their descendants move outward, changing as they form the protective cornified layer. The outer corneocytes no longer have nuclei. This combination gives a living renewing base beneath a tough exposed barrier rather than a single uniform sheet of identical cells.

check.q: Where do the epidermis's living cells obtain nutrients if no blood vessels enter the layer?
check.a: By diffusion from vessels in the underlying dermis.

steps.title: Depth changes what repair requires
steps.text:
A superficial injury can be re-covered by epithelial cells from surviving basal regions and skin appendages. A deeper injury that destroys dermal connective tissue also requires repair of the structural layer beneath the epithelium.

Fibroblasts lay down collagen in that deeper repair, producing a scar whose organisation and appendages differ from uninjured skin. Thus a closed surface does not mean that every original layer has been recreated. Relate repair to which cells and scaffolding remain, rather than simply to the surface area of the wound.

check.q: Why can a deep wound leave a lasting scar even after the epidermis has closed over it?
check.a: The damaged dermal framework is repaired with collagen-rich scar tissue rather than fully recreating its original organisation.

objectives: Name the layers of the epidermis and the dermis
Relate burn depth to the structures destroyed
Describe the appendages and where their stem cells live
Explain how an avascular epidermis is nourished and distinguish epidermal renewal from dermal repair
takeaways: Epidermis: basale, spinosum, granulosum, (lucidum), corneum.
Superficial partial-thickness burns heal from adnexal stem cells; full-thickness burns cannot.
Thick skin has a stratum lucidum and no hair follicles.
The epidermis receives nutrients by diffusion from dermal vessels; its basal cells renew the surface, while deeper injury can require dermal scar formation.
